Special Commission of Inquiry
into Healthcare Funding
Before: The Commissioner,
Mr Richard Beasley SC
At Level 2, 121 Macquarie Street,
Sydney, New South Wales
Wednesday, 29 November 2023 at 10.00am
(Day 003)
Mr Ed Muston SC (Senior Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ross Glover (Counsel Assisting)
Dr Tamsin Waterhouse (Counsel Assisting)
Also present:
Mr Richard Cheney SC with Mr Hilbert Chiu for NSW Health

THE COMMISSIONER: Yes, Mr Glover.
MR GLOVER: Thank you, Commissioner, yesterday before the
start of the evidence I handed up a tender list by way of
bulk tender. Just to ensure it is reflected in the record,
I dealt with the tender of the joint report, which is A1,
but I also, as part of that bulk tender, tender documents
which have been notionally marked as exhibits A2 to A52 in
that list.
EXHIBIT #A2-A52 BULK TENDER OF DOCUMENTS MARKED A2 TO A52
AS IDENTIFIED IN TENDER LIST
<NIGEL LYONS, on former oath: [10.02am]
<KERRY CHANT, on former affirmation: [10.02am]
<DEBORAH WILLCOX, on former affirmation: [10.02am]
MR GLOVER: Can we have the joint report
[MOH.9999.0001.0001] put up on the screen, please, and we
will go to paragraph 80.
Ms Willcox, we're still in your section of the report
so I will start directing these questions to you, but, like
yesterday, if any of Dr Chant or Dr Lyons wish to add at
any time, please feel free to do so.
In this section of the report, the concept of
preventative health is dealt with, and we touched on this a
little bit yesterday, but what I would like to do to start
today is explore what that concept is, what it involves and
how it is currently being managed within the system. What
is within the ambit of preventative health?
MS WILLCOX: Good morning and thank you. I will pass over
to Dr Chant shortly. I'll just make some initial comments.
So preventative health, as the submission highlights,
is a joint responsibility across both governments and
primary care, of course.
In NSW Health, our community health centres would be
one of the key locations where we have programs around
weight management, diet, exercise, avoidance of smoking,
alcohol and the like - those preventative measures that we
know from a very strong evidence base to keep people well

and avoid the development of chronic disease or
hospitalisation for other reasons.
We have a number of programs across the state.
There's a myriad of initiatives. We focus very much too on
the ageing and frailty, attending to issues that may lead
people to fall, so falls programs are a very common
preventative program across the state. Exercise routines
such as Tai Chi, for instance, are very popular in our
older communities in terms of keeping people strong and
balanced and well and avoiding injury from fall or frailty.
The ability to improve our interaction with patients
in more opportunistic ways across the system - so, for
instance, if a patient is coming in for surgery, they would
routinely go to a preadmission clinic. There would be
chest x-ray, perhaps, and bloods taken, but there might be
discussions around weight, smoking, mobility - anything
that can be done to contribute to a better outcome for that
surgery, for instance.
I think one of the things Dr Chant would probably want
to add to the discussion today is just how we increase that
opportunistic - I don't mean that in a pejorative sense,
but in a positive sense - how wherever we interface with
patients and consumers we can be contributing to some of
the preventative health opportunities that we can support
them with, and that they can actually do self-managed
preventative care is a very positive option. Not everybody
needs a program or a clinician to support them.
MR GLOVER: Just before I go to Dr Chant for that purpose,
you mentioned, as it is set out in the submission and in
the report, that it is a joint responsibility across
governments. How is that joint responsibility being
delivered at the moment?
MS WILLCOX: There is a National Preventative Health
Strategy, a 10-year strategy that the Commonwealth produced
along with the states, which guides some of the
population/nationwide preventative health measures that are
important to the wellbeing of the community.
I think I would probably now throw to Dr Chant to talk
in detail. It is really in her bailiwick, thank you.
DR CHANT: Thanks you very much for the question. Perhaps

just if we take it step by step through the process and we
look at some of the primary determinants of the healthy
population. They're going back to of the social
determinants of health. So the places where people live
and work can really influence health. For instance, if we
have reduced travel times, we have more time for leisure,
physical activity, able to have time to prepare meals.
If we have walkable parks that are safe, well lit, we
reduce social isolation, promote physical activity. So the
environments in which we live can shape, can be a positive
factor that can support people to adopt those healthy
behaviours and lifestyles.
Government also has a key role in regulation, so
setting things like tobacco regulation. We've heard
recently Minister Butler that has announced the
Commonwealth reforms in e-cigarettes. So regulation is
also a whole of government initiative and those things can
enable a health-promoting environment in which we live.
In terms of primary care - this goes to the joint
responsibility across governments - primary care is an
important setting for prevention. Things like the regular
health checks, skin checks, cancer screening, all of those
things are important, as well as regular blood pressure
checks, management of high cholesterol.
These are preventable risk factors that can be
modified by, in some cases, advice around healthy diet,
maintaining healthy weight, physical activity, as well as,
in some cases, it may require medication or more formal
treatment. So that's again a pivotal role of general
practice.
We then perhaps can categorise a set of conditions
whereby they're more likely to be secondary prevention, so
people already have disease, but we know that even smoking
reduction in someone that already has lung disease can slow
progression, or heart disease, quitting smoking can
actually improve outcomes quite radically. So this would
be, for instance, things that primary care would do, but
that also may occur in our system where people are touching
our system, be it for cancer diagnosis, heart diagnosis,
lung diagnosis, those conversations around smoking
cessation and supporting people to quit smoking.

We also have, for instance, very good evidence that
physical activity, if you're on cancer treatment, actually
can improve your outcome. So again, incorporating some of
these lifestyle modification programs within our care
pathway is actually strongly evidence based and --
MR GLOVER: I'm sorry to cut you off, just from that
answer, do I understand it that primary care is
a significant deliverer, if I could put it that way, of
preventative health?
DR CHANT: Yes. Primary care is the first port of call
who would do the majority of the clinical preventative
care, as I have described that more whole of government
prevention sort of setting, but in terms of clinical
engagement around primary/secondary prevention, clearly
primary health care is very heavy lifter in that space
MR GLOVER: Although when people come into hospital, there
are other opportunities to deliver preventative health
measures to improve their overall health and outcomes.
DR CHANT: That's correct, and for some of our services
also we provide access to those that may not be connected
to primary care. We talked earlier yesterday about some of
the barriers to accessing primary care, be they
rural/regional and distribution of general practice, all
the way through to the fact that the client may not have
financial means, transport.
So our services provide an opportunity for engagement
in that broader health promotion, with the aim ideally to
connect them back to a primary care setting, but in the
meantime, it presents opportunities for us to look at
tobacco cessation, we may look at other screening, and
addressing immediate - whilst we're addressing other health
concerns of the individual, it's an opportunity for us to
do other preventative care, including things like
immunisation as well.
MR GLOVER: How well is primary care delivering those
preventative health services?
DR CHANT: I think primary care is doing a lot of the
heavy lifting. I would just like to say, if we look at our
vaccination coverage for our under 5s, which I described
yesterday, we have around 95 per cent immunisation coverage

when we get to that five-year mark. The vast majority in
New South Wales context is done by general practice.
So general practice is obviously doing a lot of the
heavy lifting in this respect. You may hear from them
about whether the funding adequately supports the focus on
prevention, whether the funding supports the full scope of
other multidisciplinary practitioners in their practice
taking their full scope - for instance, things like nurses
being able to claim potentially Medicare benefits for the
immunisation independently would be an example where that
scope might be considered safe and appropriate. So there
might be other roles that could be done in a broader
multidisciplinary team. I think you'll hear some of those
comments if you engage with the primary care practitioners.
THE COMMISSIONER: The MBS items and the fee for service
that have been direct or created to provide pathways for
preventative health like the GP management plans and things
of that nature - are you aware of published evaluations
about those, about what the outcomes have been from those
changes to the MBS over the last 20-odd years?
DR CHANT: I think we could provide some evidence perhaps
around some of the health-screening items more in the
Aboriginal health - the introduction of the 715 health
screening, and some of the evaluations.
DR LYONS: To answer your question, Commissioner, I'm not
aware of any evaluation around those particular changes to
the MBS that you referred to, and that's something we could
investigate further.
THE COMMISSIONER: You read many reviews, including from
the Productivity Commission, which will analyse or provide
opinions regarding ABF and fee for service and say neither
really promotes preventative health measures. Then
I think, or imagine, to address that, items have gone on
the MBS - you know, like the management plans I mentioned.
I either haven't found or haven't had brought to my
attention how effective these things are. Bearing in mind,
I think, the reports also say that for any preventative
health measure, getting the evidence is difficult, partly
because it is such long term.
DR LYONS: That is an ongoing challenge. I think if you
look at these things in totality, episodic care, such as

the opportunities that we have to intervene when people are
with our services are not the best place - they are an
important opportunity to promote healthy lifestyles and
activities that will improve outcomes for people and
changes, but a lot of those changes require individuals to
have behavioural change over a longer term. That needs to
be through a reinforcement and support for those changes in
an ongoing relationship, which is where primary care is
best placed to deliver that.
I think we need to look at these things in the context
of the health promotion activities that we can do for a
community at population health level, which carry very much
a primary prevention, and then there's the secondary
prevention in which we all have a very big part to play.
Secondary prevention is very much where we believe our
services should focus their activities certainly in the
acute settings at least.
THE COMMISSIONER: Thanks.
MR GLOVER: Picking up on one of the Commissioner's
questions, I take it that some preventative health
activities take a long time to see the benefit in the
system; would that be right?
DR CHANT: Some do but some don't.
MR GLOVER: Are there some examples of more immediate
results?
DR CHANT: Yes. For instance, we know that the role of
primary care, particularly in STI screening, is probably
a very classic example, where diagnosing sexually
transmitted infections and effectively treating those,
where there is an effective treatment. That is a classic
example.
Vaccination, where we know that if you vaccinated for
the flu season, you're going to reduce your admissions to
hospital for those that have been identified as requiring
the vaccination. So there's a clear link.
Tobacco cessation, as I said, although it provides
a longer term, we know that even stopping tobacco smoking
prior to surgery will improve your postoperative recovery.
So for many things, it can be quite short term.

But what is important is we also have very strong
evidence that changing those behaviours will change
long-term outcomes. So we don't actually need to do the
long-term outcomes; we know in itself that if weave helped
someone quit smoking, that we don't then need to measure,
because we can draw on other studies that show that that's
beneficial for them to be off smoking.
MR GLOVER: Those are measures that not only improve the
health of the individual but do they also reduce demand
over time on the public hospital system?
DR CHANT: Yes, they do, because we know that many of
those risk factors cause a multiplicity of chronic
diseases, and what we would be aiming to do is to support
people to live healthier lives, chronic disease free lives.
MR GLOVER: To the extent that preventative care is
delivered in the public hospital system, how is that
funded? Is that wholly funded by the state or is there
a Commonwealth contribution to it?
DR CHANT: It would be picked up under the activity based
funding system and then there are particular payment
programs.
DR LYONS: There are programs that are funded centrally.
Those are funded through a block, often, through specific
programs that are directed towards health promotion
activities and prevention activities.
THE COMMISSIONER: Are these short-term programs or
time-limited programs?
DR LYONS: No, they are actually ongoing, and things like
the work we do on screening programs and --
MS WILLCOX: "Munch & move".
DR LYONS: "Munch & Move".
DR CHANT: They are probably different in state based
funding. There's a number of shared screening programs
that we would have a role in, so bowel cancer,
BreastScreen. The part we pay in the funding varies. For
instance, in the mammography, I understand - we will have

to check - it's a shared funding arrangement with the
Commonwealth, in terms of that. But we may fund some
additional work on targeting those that are hard to reach
or where participation in the program is identified to be
less than usual, and in that's specific programs.
DR LYONS: There are those specific programs. But then
the other components would be included in the care
activities that are occurring that would be funded through
activity. There is not a specific component of that that
I am aware of that relates to prevention; it is considered
to be in the totality of that care and funded through those
activity arrangements.
DR CHANT: In relation to some of the state funding
programs, there is funding, as Ms Willcox said, for some
programs in the childhood space. We work in partnership
with education, but we do a lot of work in early childhood
settings. A program called Munch & Move which again is
trying to educate and support healthier eating and physical
activity that's appropriate in that setting.
We also work in partnership with schools. We do work
with curriculum in schools to support education incorporate
health in all its dimensions and, most recently, we've been
doing some work to embed, for instance, e-cigarettes, in
age-appropriate guidance on e-cigarettes within the health
curriculum in schools.
So they're just examples of state funded programs that
really address this work. We've also done some work around
healthy canteens in schools and supported education in
that. Again, a lot of those have been programs that have
been supported by whole of government approach. There has
been a recognition around the focus on young children and
recognition that some of the trajectory for the risk
factors of being above a healthy weight and not physically
active are set very early. So again, it supports the work
in this early intervention space particularly for families.
THE COMMISSIONER: Can I just ask a question I should know
the answer to but I don't, so I have to ask the question.
In the Productivity Commission's "Shifting the Dial" review
back in August 2017, when it was dealing with the issue of
the topic of changes to hospital funding, in relation to
activity based funding, it said this:

If there are better ways of changing
activity-based funding to give [local
health networks] or [primary health
networks] the incentives to improve health
status, and avoid hospitalisations,
hospital durations and other health care
costs, then implement [them].
It said:
One way of formalising a new approach
would be to establish a Prevention and
Chronic Condition Prevention and Management
Fund ... in each local health district with
both the Australian Government and ...
state governments [contributing].
Did that happen?
DR LYONS: Not to my knowledge.
THE COMMISSIONER: Can I also ask this, just while we're
on this topic. Again, I don't know the answer to this but
I probably should. I'm sure you would be aware, there was
a Queensland review a few years back, it must have been
right in the middle of the pandemic, "Unleashing the
potential: an open and equitable health system". Are you
aware of that review?
DR LYONS: Not the detail of it, Commissioner
THE COMMISSIONER: It was published in August 2020, so it
was right in the middle of the pandemic. But one of the
recommendations was to amend what would be the equivalent
of our Health Services Act to add prevention and population
health as activities and responsibilities for the LHDs, our
equivalent of LHDs. I know it's not in the Act but is that
incorporated in the service agreements?
DR LYONS: It has always been - I won't talk to the
details, but --
THE COMMISSIONER: It might depend on how you read the
functions under the Act as to whether it's incorporated
already.
DR LYONS: Yes. Certainly it's a component of the

responsibilities of the local health districts and always
has been, under all of the arrangements, that we have
a responsibility to the community to keep them healthy and
well as well as to treat illness and diseases, so --
THE COMMISSIONER: You say that's broad enough to include
prevention?
DR LYONS: Absolutely.
THE COMMISSIONER: And that's the way it has been
interpreted?
DR LYONS: Absolutely. And, yes, there population health
teams, public health teams, health promotion teams that
exist within the local health districts that have that
focus.
THE COMMISSIONER: That might be a case - well, I won't
say it. Maybe it was a case of Queensland catching up with
New South Wales already. Who knows.
MR GLOVER: If we just go ahead to paragraph 174 in the
report, please. There in the first line of 174:
Preventive services and early interventions
should be strong pillars of Australia’s
healthcare system ...
Are they currently?
DR CHANT: I think I would answer that question by saying
Australia does really well. Our infant mortality rates are
low, our life expectancy is one of the top - in the top
three of the world. So we do well. Can we do more and
with the rebalancing towards chronic disease, does that put
additional challenges where we need to refocus on
prevention, I would argue yes.
THE COMMISSIONER: Living longer is just one issue. The
real issue, especially for the cost of the health system,
is living long but if you're living longer with chronic
disease, then that's expensive.
DR CHANT: That's correct.
THE COMMISSIONER: And not great for people, either.

DR CHANT: And not great, yes, that's right. So I think
what we would really want to look at is making sure that
people had lived very healthy lives into age, but healthy,
active lives that were mentally challenging and socially
inclusive.
So whilst I comment on length of life, I suppose I can
give you a whole range of metrics that we actually do well
in - disability adjusted life years lost, all of those
metrics. I think we need to position Australia as well -
we have adopted a lot of prevention screening programs, we
have rolled out a lot of vaccines, we have had a lot of
access to those things.
Do we need to do more? I would say yes. Do we need
to align - I suppose we need to think about the challenges
that are laid out by the way the burden of disease has
changed and we need to pivot and evolve our funding systems
and our systems to deal with the challenges facing us. But
it's not only a health issue. I hope you've heard from the
testimony we've given that, really, this is a whole of
government issue and it cuts across multiple levels of
government.
DR LYONS: Just to use a single example which I think is
illustrative. If we had people that were all a healthy
weight, we would hugely reduce the burden of both
osteoarthritis and musculoskeletal conditions, and that
leads to joint replacement surgeries, which have a huge
impact; and also diabetes, which has huge implications for
the costs of delivering health care and implications for
people in terms of living healthy lives. Just that one
change alone - and it would have other flow-on effects to
other conditions as well.
DR CHANT: Cancer, cardiovascular disease.
DR LYONS: Cancer and a lot of other things. But that is
one example that that is not just a health issue, that's
a whole of society issue.
THE COMMISSIONER: Can I just ask two things that flow
from that. One, I fully accept that best preventative
health measures, plans, programs, aren't defined
necessarily by how much money is spent on them, it's how
well they are designed and then implemented, because it's

so complex. But we've heard various figures or percentages
about how much either Australia or New South Wales spends
on preventative health as a percentage of total health
expenditure. So I've seen 2 per cent, I've seen larger
than 2 per cent. The Productivity Commission, I'm sure
I have seen, Australia-wide, 1.5 per cent, with other
equivalent relatively First World nations higher. Is there
a definitive figure as to how much either New South Wales
or Australia spends on preventative health as a percentage
of the health spend?
DR CHANT: There are definitions that are meant to capture
it, but it's actually very difficult to do so, and there
has to be caution applied in any comparisons. I'll give
you an example.
In New South Wales, we have reasonably high levels of
water fluoridation which prevents dental caries, which
prevents other issues. That is funded and supported, local
councils do that, and there is a subsidy provided by
government to councils for the renewal of the plants and we
support local councils to implement that. That would be
different in other states and territories. I have talked
about some of the --
THE COMMISSIONER: That's an example of preventative
health, though, where the population or the people don't
have to do anything because it's in the water.
DR LYONS: Yes.
DR CHANT: But there are costs. There are cost associated
with renewal of the infrastructure and supporting the
councils with that, so that's a choice with that.
I suppose my point was the boundaries of how you capture it
and define it are very challenging and various estimates
are there.
Another example, for instance, is there's good
evidence around brief interventions for tobacco and, as
I said, how do we capture everything, every time our
doctors, interns, residents are doing that? But there's
really good evidence and it only needs to be a one-minute
line to reinforce the importance and then the GP following
up.
THE COMMISSIONER: Tobacco is an example where someone

does have to do something - you have to stop smoking. But
to go, I think, to both of your points, Dr Lyons and
Dr Chant, about whole of government, there has been a whole
of government approach to tobacco because of the changes to
advertising. In the course of my life, it used to be
Paul Hogan on TV. Now there is no TV, there is no sports
sponsorships, plain paper packaging. I'll just forget to
raise it if I don't continue, but what we're told is, in
terms of prevention, how important obesity is, because it
leads to so many --
DR CHANT: Issues, yes.
THE COMMISSIONER: -- different health conditions. I was
reading the other day that in the last - it might only be
since 1992, maybe, Britain has had 20 or more obesity
plans. But that's where whole of government is important
because it's one thing for NSW Health to develop a plan,
but if people are inundated with advertising for processed
foods and sugary drinks, it's very difficult for health to
get much traction in a prevention plan. Is that
a reasonable observation?
MS WILLCOX: Yes. I think it goes to a number of the
things that Dr Chant talked about yesterday and touched on
this morning around - urban planning is a very important
area. I know that Dr Chant will talk to this but the NSW
Food Authority and labelling of foods and enabling people
to make the right choices when they go into a supermarket
is not necessarily that easy, the way labelling is done and
I know there is work with the Food Authority.
DR CHANT: And health ministers. So I think tackling
people being above healthy weight is a major issue for us,
and also getting people physically active as well. So we
want to also focus on the multiple risk factors. As I've
defined, there's a lot of enablers for that which sit
outside government.
But health has a key role in advocacy or presenting
the evidence or working with its partners, and there has
actually been a lot of work on obesity, particularly
childhood obesity, in New South Wales. We've rolled out
height and weight measures and linkage to care. We've got
programs that I've articulated.
We've got a program in maternity services called "Get

Healthy in Pregnancy". So women are supported through with
specialist practitioner support to maintain healthy weight
and diet and exercise through pregnancy. That has been
well adopted through a health coaching model. So there are
a range of initiatives, but you're correct in saying that
to tackle these very complex issues, it does require whole
of government and a discussion with the community around
how do we work together. This is really going to have to
be a partnership between all levels of government,
industry and people --
THE COMMISSIONER: And it's also a preventative health
measure, without needing to go into the details, I think,
where there's opposition because of commercial interests,
or retail --
DR CHANT: There are particular views around that, but
I hope that you've taken it from our perspective that we
believe that individuals and communities need to be
supported with enabling environment and recognise that
there are barriers for people to take up the behaviour. So
it's not around making it an issue for the individual; it's
really seeing it as a community and a place-based and whole
of government response.
MR GLOVER: Just in paragraph 175:
Low proportional investment in preventive
health, the wider determinants of health
and increasing burden of chronic disease
has led to increased spending on
treatments to manage conditions that could
be prevented ...
et cetera. By that, do we understand that historically,
the focus on those things hasn't been as you would want it,
as of now?
DR LYONS: Our system has been responding to the demand it
sees in treating patients who are unwell. That has been
the focus of hospitals and the local health district
service over many years, and that increasing demand we're
seeing means that to respond to it increasingly we're
putting resources into those emergency departments,
hospitalisations, surgeries that people need, to make sure
we can treat people.

So we've tended to focus on invest engine that side,
proportionally, at a proportionally greater level, because
of the need and demand, and I think what we're signalling
is there needs to be a shift over time to get more
proportional spending into the prevention space. But
that's not just a state issue. That's for everybody
involved in designing and delivering health services in
this country.
MR GLOVER: Are there challenges in making that shift
whilst also catering to the current demands on the public
health system?
DR LYONS: Absolutely. That's the challenge we're
highlighting and the need for a refocusing. I mean, we
shouldn't be taking away from those really important
services we provide around treating people with disease.
We do it very well. We need to keep that focus, but we
need to proportionally spend more on the prevention side.
MS WILLCOX: It's probably why - it is not "probably", it
is why you've seen and heard from, I'm sure, many people,
including us, about the work around integrated care, caring
for chronic and complex patients and how we try and keep
people out of hospital and support them in the home. We
have made a significant shift.
Integrated care activities such as Dr Lyons referred
to, with people that might require a knee replacement, with
osteoarthritis, can now go to a clinic and with an exercise
regime and often weight support, can avoid actually having
knee surgery and we can take people off the wait list for
surgery.
So the system has been innovative in terms of
identifying different pathways to provide care and to try
to mitigate the risk of somebody ending up in hospital with
a chronic and complex condition that could be managed in
the home or in a community-based setting. So it has been
the driver for much of this work.
MR GLOVER: This integration that you speak of is not just
within the public hospital network but across primary care
settings as well, is it?
DR CHANT: That's correct. It's very important that,
regardless of the two levels of government that are

funders, that we actually run a seamless system for the
patients, that the patient actually can move between it and
that our services adjust for the services where they're
best delivered. As we spoke about yesterday, primary
health practitioners being the integrator and the
fundamental providers of primary prevention, but we provide
evidence-based care that really is supportive and
introduces and incorporates prevention that supports the
work of the primary health care practitioner.
DR LYONS: We have signalled this direction through
a number of changes we have made, and one of them was
mentioned yesterday - the agreement we've reached with the
primary health networks across the state.
Historically, we've run parallel systems almost and
where patients get referred between them, and what we're
saying is we need to turn that around to have a one system
mindset, that we're the one health system, no matter where
people are in it, they are supported with information, with
a range of activities that will enable them to receive
optimal care in any of those settings, but it's joined up.
That has been the challenge up until now and we need to
refocus what we do, but we need other parts of the system
to change as well.
DR CHANT: I'd just like to comment, so that's the sort of
general approach, but there are then some services that we
run in the health system that see very vulnerable groups of
patients, where it's actually taken quite a lot of time to
build trust for them to come and access our services. That
creates an incredible opportunity for us to have that
broader discussion. So they may be coming in to us with
drug and alcohol or mental health issues, but that gives us
an opportunity, as we're addressing the drug and alcohol
concerns, to actually screen them for other things, offer
them vaccination, potentially address their broader health
issues, all the time looking at transference to a primary
care practitioner. But for a period of time, due to that
fact that they may have faced stigma and discrimination,
they may have felt very uncomfortable attending the primary
care. It will need a bit more intensive work for us to
support them where we might be providing services which are
more in the primary care domain for a discrete group of

that means those patients will end up in the public system
on our waiting lists for our patient care or in our
emergency departments.
MR GLOVER: Is the inability to regulate that's being
referred to in subparagraph (e) pointing to an inability of
NSW Health to influence those types of circumstances?
DR LYONS: We have no control over any of those
circumstances. We are completely powerless on that and
just respond to the situation.
MR GLOVER: Aside from driving demand into the public
health system, are there any other impacts on the delivery
of care by those circumstances?
DR CHANT: I think it's really important that when we look
at disparities in access, conditions that are particularly
elective - what might be seen as more elective in nature -
can be amplified because access to those procedures occurs
through largely a specialist system, so this just
contributes to some of the inequities of access.
MR GLOVER: Finally, to paragraph 212. Dr Lyons, you,
I think, referred perhaps yesterday to the development of
health hubs that are referred to in this paragraph. What
do you have in mind by a health hub?
DR LYONS: I think I outlined some of the concepts, which
are collocation of services that the state provides with
services that might be provided by other providers.
MR GLOVER: Are there examples in existence now?
DR LYONS: We have some examples. They're not widespread,
and what we would like to see is building on those that
currently exist, evaluating their effectiveness and making

them more systematised in terms of the delivery of those
types of models. Part of it is the capital that's
available to do that. We need to probably think about the
types of facilities that we actually have available for
people to work from and whether or not we can support more
of those being delivered.
MR GLOVER: These are different to MPSs?
DR LYONS: Yes. They wouldn't have inpatient care, for
instance, they would be focused on delivering care in
community settings and allowing the multidisciplinary team,
whether that's our teams or the teams that exist in primary
care groups, diagnostics services, whether that's pathology
or imaging, some specialists, allied health and medical
specialists to be available in the one setting to enable
that holistic care around the patient and ensuring that the
patient wasn't asked to go from one place to another, to
another, to another, to another to ensure that they could -
you would have pharmacy services on the site as well, so
you would be able to provide a one-stop shop.
What we hear from many patients is an advantage coming
to an emergency department is that it is a one-stop shop.
You get all those things together and if you need
medications, they'll be provided to you in the acute
circumstances as well. So replicating that type of model
to enable people to access holistic care and be treated
effectively in the one space is the sort of model we're
talking about.
MR GLOVER: In terms of funding, would that be wholly
funded by the state or would there be a Commonwealth
contribution?
DR LYONS: Ideally there'd be a contribution from the
Commonwealth as well, particularly for the services that
are existing on the Commonwealth side.
MR GLOVER: Is there a barrier to, if the state was
delivering general practitioner type services, receiving
funding under the MBS?
DR LYONS: If we are salarying the doctors, there
is section 19(2), I think, of the agreement, which says
that people can't access an MBS benefit unless there's an
application made and there are certain criteria that need

to be met for that to be agreed to. So salaried doctors
would be an, issue. But if they're doctors who are working
within the MBS arrangements they can access those payments.
MR GLOVER: There are some examples, aren't there, of
those exemptions having been granted?
DR LYONS: There are. We have examples of things like the
single employer model in the Murrumbidgee where that's to
support general practice training and ensuring that
ultimately GPs are retained within rural communities.
MR GLOVER: Just briefly describe that model.
DR LYONS: It's a model where rather than - so for most of
the specialty training in our system, specialists are
trained within the public health system, apart from general
practice. So nearly all of the other specialties are
trained within our services.
General practice is unique in that people train in
general practice settings, which are outside of our
responsibility. So historically we've had no
responsibility after the first couple of years of
graduation, and then people will choose to do general
practice training.
Part of that is that they relinquish the employment
arrangements they have with the system, the state, and go
into an arrangement where they negotiate contracts of
employment with the various supervisors in those practices.
What we heard from trainees, and the reason it drove
the single employer model, was that that was a barrier for
people who were just graduating and embarking on a career,
that they lose the certainty of entitlements of an
employment arrangement and have to go into a contracted
arrangement, which is not ideal.
Having the single employer model enabled the
candidates who wanted to go into that training to feel more
confident about going into that training, because they knew
they were in an employment arrangement that went for the
length of time they would be in training, and enabled the
services to support them as they went through that training
and with a view that, at the end of that training, the
practitioners would want to stay in those environments and

continue to work with those skills.
MR GLOVER: In addition to the training benefits, there
are also the benefits in having services on the ground to
be delivered to the community?
DR LYONS: Absolutely.
MR GLOVER: Is that model being expanded?
DR LYONS: Yes, through the success of that model, which
emanated in the Murrumbidgee, the Commonwealth have
supported that expansion, and we are looking at expanding
that right across the state into the rural and regional
settings across the state.
MR GLOVER: Is that another example of being able to
develop this hub model of care?
DR LYONS: It's an example of innovation and developing
new ways of doing things that require flexibility.
Ultimately, it could lead to the development of these hubs,
but it doesn't necessarily, of itself, lead to those
outcomes.
